1:
The chapter opens on a difficulty nobody evades: a marriage the law forbids, said to be of the Lord. Clarke restricts the phrase as narrowly as it will go — God permitted it, and in no other sense can we understand the words. Ellicott says much the same, that all it can mean is that God overruled events to further his own designs, making the fierceness of men redound to his praise; and he sets beside it the sense of divine rule found even in heathen writers, quoting the opening of the Iliad, where amid all the crimes and passions of men the counsel of Zeus is accomplished. Gill takes the opposite view: Samson himself knew it was of the Lord, his desire not arising from carnal affection — she was not so very fair, and her younger sister was fairer — but from the Spirit urging him to it and showing the occasion it would give against the Philistines, which he did not disclose to his parents. Henry resolves it a third way, denying the case is exemplary at all. Samson was himself a riddle, a paradox of a man, who did what was great and good by what seemed weak and evil, being designed as no pattern to us, who must walk by rule and not example, but a type of him who knew no sin and was made sin for us. Ellicott adds a grammatical warning: some explain the one who sought a quarrel to be Jehovah, which he thinks most unlikely.

That the marriage was against the law is agreed, but Keil states the law precisely and finds a gap. Only marriages with Canaanite women are expressly prohibited in the passages usually cited, so a Philistine bride falls outside the letter — though the parents' aversion is well founded, since the reason of the prohibition covers her. Ellicott approaches it from feeling rather than statute, observing that uncircumcised was a term of peculiar hatred on Israelite lips, and pointing to Shechem for how repugnant the match would seem to Manoah and his wife. Henry puts the incongruity plainly: shall a Nazarite devoted to the Lord covet to become one with a worshipper of Dagon, on no evidence she was wise or virtuous, but because something in her face was agreeable to his fancy?

The reason Samson gives is that she is right in his eyes, and Clarke will not let it pass. This, he says, is what passes for sufficient warrant in the random choice of a wife or husband, and he quotes the couplet — thou art all beauty, or all blindness I. Where the will has power enough, its determinations become their own rule of right; and he compares the maxim to the motto cast on the brass ordnance of Louis the Fourteenth, the last argument of kings, which he glosses as meaning that his will backed by such instruments shall be the rule of right and wrong. Such logic, he remarks, is now suspected, and is not likely to be generally received again without violent demonstration.

On the town itself Gill and Ellicott raise the same small difficulty independently, that Judah is elsewhere said to have gone up to Timnath where Samson goes down to it. Gill reports the rival solutions — two towns of the name, one an ascent and one a descent, or one so situated that those approaching from one side climbed and from the other descended — and follows the authority preferring the first; Ellicott leaves it open, noting that the site still keeps the name and that the word means a portion. Clarke supplies the later history, that David took the place from the Philistines and that they held it again under Ahaz, and Gill that it lay twelve miles from where Samson lived.
5:
The lion is handled two ways. Clarke insists the feat was not natural: nothing intimates he did it by his own strength, but by the Spirit coming mightily upon him, so that the might was neither his own nor at his command, being attached by God's will to his hair and his Nazarite state. Ellicott moves the opposite way, collecting parallels until the exploit looks heroic rather than impossible — Josephus says he throttled the beast, meaning his Greek readers to think of Hercules; Pausanias records an athlete who killed a lion unarmed at Olympus; Arabs have done the same; and David and Benaiah did it before him. He adds that the verb rendered came mightily means rather pervaded, the same word used of the evil spirit that rushed upon Saul. He also shows lions were then common, arguing from place-names — Lebaoth meaning lionesses, Shaalbim jackals, Zeboim hyenas — and describes the vineyards, on hills once terraced to the summit like Italian valleys and now bleak from the denudation of centuries, though labour might make them fruitful again. Henry allegorises: young people do not consider how they expose themselves to the lion that seeks to devour when they wander from pious parents, nor what lions lurk in vineyards — the vineyards of red wines — and since Christ has conquered that roaring lion, believers like Samson find honey in the carcass.

The bees drew an objection, and the answers are the most interesting thing in the chapter. Clarke treats the ancient belief as support, quoting the fourth Georgic at length on the swarm that rose from an opened ox and reasoning that such a thing was not infrequent. Ellicott takes the same passage and uses it against him: the notion that bees are generated in rotting oxen is a vulgar error, and bees do hate all putrescence — but the word rendered carcase means skeleton, the fierce Eastern sun reduces a body to dried bones rapidly, and bees have no objection to those. He supplies two cases: the head of Onesilus, hung over the gates of Amathus, which a swarm filled with combs, and bees building between the skeletons of two sisters buried at Verona. Keil reaches the same mechanism but draws the line elsewhere, denying that a mere skeleton is meant, since bees would not hive in one, and holding that the body was dried by the sun without putrefying — in the Arabian desert, he reports, a fallen man or camel may be dried out within a day.

Whether Samson broke his vow by taking the honey is disputed on the same ground. Gill exculpates him: on Josephus's account he took three pieces of comb and ate as he walked, which he could do without touching the carcase and so defiling himself, of which as a Nazarite he had to be especially careful. Ellicott concedes nothing: unless a skeleton is no dead body, he could not have done it without breaking the express conditions of his vow. On why he told nobody, Keil says his parents would have refused the honey as unclean and would have known the riddle's answer; Ellicott offers three reasons — his reticence, their greater scrupulousness, and the possibility that he had already framed the riddle and would give no clue.

Smaller matters divide them in the same pattern. On the interval before the wedding, Gill and Clarke both supply a year, Gill adding that twelve months were allowed the bride to prepare; Ellicott declines the precision, the phrase meaning only after days and being used elsewhere of many years. On the talking with the woman, Ellicott insists it cannot mean talked about her, since Eastern custom would not have allowed the conversation unless his parents had gone before; Gill entertains the very reading Ellicott rejects, that it may refer to the father speaking about her to her relations.
10:
Henry approves the feast on principle. Though a Nazarite, Samson did not affect singularity but did as young men did on such occasions; it is no part of religion to go contrary to the innocent usages of the places where we live, and a reproach to religion when its professors give others just occasion to call them covetous, sneaking and morose. A good man, he says, should strive to make himself in the best sense a good companion.

Why thirty companions were fetched is less agreed. Keil takes the bride's relations to have invited them, as children of the bride-chamber, since Samson had brought none. Ellicott draws an inference from that absence — it seems to prove the marriage was highly unpopular among his countrymen — and adds that thirty was a most unusual number. Henry offers two readings and prefers the darker: seeing what a comely man he was they may have brought them to do him honour, or rather, seeing how strong he was, they brought them seemingly as companions but really as a guard, or spies to observe him. Keil and Ellicott then reject the same variant independently. The Greek and Josephus render the clause when they were afraid of him, which requires an altered reading; Ellicott calls it unwarranted, and Keil objects that fear of Samson suits neither the facts nor the following words that they were with him, which must then be paraphrased most arbitrarily as they watched him.

The riddle sets them collecting parallels. Clarke reports the Greek custom of enigmas at festivals, where the solver won a crown or a goblet of wine and those who failed drank at one draught, without drawing breath and with hands tied, a large portion of water or wine mixed with brine. Ellicott derives the Hebrew word from a root meaning to knot, and gathers the riddles of Solomon with the Queen of Sheba and with Hiram, the boy Abdemon who helped one king as the sage Bias helped another, and the Sphinx that devoured those who could not answer; since large sums hung on the solution, such riddles were much of the nature of wagers.

All agree the riddle was not fair, and for the same reason. Clarke says that unless the fact it refers to were known there is no rule by which it could be found out, and thinks it was in verse, the two clauses preserving its order. Ellicott confesses it hardly fair, the event alluded to being most unusual and nobody able to guess it without a clue — and quotes Shakespeare, that it is seldom the bee leaves her comb in the dead carrion. Yet Ellicott defends the terms of the wager as generous, since each companion needed find only one shirt and one robe while Samson, if they guessed, owed thirty. He adds a North German legend of a woman offered her husband's life if she could set a riddle the judges could not solve, who had found a dead horse with a bird's nest and six young in it and asked how she took the living out of the dead — and translates the old lines himself, apologising for the rendering.

On the word rendered sheets, Ellicott and Keil agree it means an undergarment of fine linen, the kind only the wealthy wore, while Clarke identifies it with the Arab hayk in which the easterner wraps himself as a Highlander in his plaid, quotes a traveller on Moorish dress, and observes that eastern dress has scarcely changed in two thousand years. On the reading Clarke notes without comment that the Syriac and Arabic have bitter where our text has strong; Ellicott refuses it, denying the word can be strained so far. Gill notes the Targum reads that the father went down about the business of the woman.
15:
A chronological knot opens the passage, and four solutions are on offer. The threat is delivered on the seventh day, yet the wife is said to have wept the seven days; and Gill reports that the Greek, Syriac and Arabic versions cut the difficulty by reading the fourth day. He himself prefers the rabbis' explanation, that the day named is the sabbath rather than the seventh of the feast, and adds a proposal ascribed to Abarbinel, that there were fourteen days in all, seven before the festival and seven during. Keil denies there is any discrepancy to solve: the woman had come with her entreaties every day out of simple curiosity, and Samson had resisted until the seventh, when the threat made her more urgent than ever. Ellicott offers the same harmony as a second option, having first noted that the margin allows the sense of the rest of the seven days.

Ellicott alone weighs both parties. If Samson appears in no favourable light here, he says, the Philistines show themselves most mean, treacherous and brutal — and he observes that the threat to burn the woman and her father's house was afterwards carried out, while the phrase about taking what they have is stronger in the Hebrew, meaning to make them paupers. On the marriage itself he is drier still: the riddle made this ill-starred wedding one of the most embittered and least joyous that ever fell to a bridegroom's lot, a just punishment for lawless fancies though God overruled it to his own ends, and a weeping, teasing bride with sullen guests might have served as warning that Philistine marriages were not good for the sons of Israel.

Why Samson yielded on the last day, and how far his wife is to be blamed, are treated gently by one and harshly by another. Ellicott suggests he hoped that telling her so late would leave no opportunity to betray him, quotes the prophet's warning to keep the door of one's mouth from her that lies in one's bosom, and enters a qualification in her favour — she might perhaps have told in any case, but she now had the excuse of violent menaces. Clarke allows her nothing: she wept not through any love to him, for it appears she had none, but to oblige her paramours, and of this he soon had ample proof.

That last word points to the real dispute, which is over the proverb Samson answers with. Clarke takes it as a direct charge of adultery — if his wife had not been unfaithful to his bed she would not have been unfaithful to his secret, and the companions being her paramours, their interest was more precious to her than her husband's. He supports it with a wall of classical parallels in which ploughing another man's ground is the standing euphemism, quoting Theognis against the man who wishes to plough in another's field, Plautus on the husband who tills a neighbour's farm and leaves his own uncultivated, and Martial on the wife who goes on bearing children while her husband is abroad; and he reports that the Greek version, the Syriac and Rabbi Levi all understood the words in this sense. Ellicott refuses it in one sentence: many commentators, following that same rabbi, find in the phrase an implication that Samson suspected his wife, but there is no sufficient reason for the view. Keil declines the question altogether, calling it a proverbial saying whose meaning is perfectly clear — which, given how far the other two are apart, is itself an answer of a kind. Ellicott adds only that the companions gave their reply in the same rhythmical form as the riddle, and Gill that they brought it in before sunset, and so in time to escape the forfeit they would otherwise have owed.
19:
The killing at Ashkelon is defended by one commentator and left standing by another. Keil argues from the order of the narrative that revenge was not the motive: the deed is ascribed to the Spirit of the Lord coming upon Samson because it showed the Philistines the superior power of the servants of Jehovah, and the text says his anger was kindled only after the thing was done — and then not against the Philistines he had paid, but against his wife who had betrayed him. Ellicott offers no such defence and declines the question, remarking only that the morality of the act can of course be judged only from the standpoint of the time. He does supply an ingenious conjecture about the occasion: since linen robes and rich garments would not be worn every day, Samson probably seized the opportunity of some great feast to Dagon, or even of another wedding, when men would be dressed in the very things he needed — and those who received the wager, he adds, had no idea where the means of paying it had come from.

What exactly was taken is less settled than it looks. Ellicott notes that the word for spoil is rendered armour in the book of Samuel, that the Greek has a word for a full panoply, and that the Targum seems to understand suits of armour. Clarke assumes clothing throughout and identifies the pieces from the modern eastern wardrobe he had described earlier, the hayk and the caftan; Keil takes them simply as the garments stripped from the slain.

The giving away of the wife is judged from two directions. Keil lays the blame on her family and makes it the decisive act: Samson went home enraged without taking her, but he did not intend to break the marriage tie, as the next chapter plainly shows; so that instead of considering the wrong he felt himself to have suffered, and trying to mitigate his anger, her parents made the breach irreparable by giving her to another. Gill states the other side without endorsing it, that the father gave her with her own consent, both of them affronted at being left, and judging her not merely injured but thereby discharged and free to marry. Ellicott and Keil agree that the man she was given to was the chief of the bridal companions, the friend of the bridegroom, one of the thirty Samson had been given at the feast. Ellicott then does something creditable: having dismissed the suspicion that Samson's proverb charged his wife with adultery, he reports without concealment a rendering of Bunsen's that would revive it, making the companion the one whose friend she had been — and concludes that whether or not the suspicion is founded, treachery and secret hostility were plainly at work.

Clarke ends the chapter on the secret rather than the marriage, and the moral is aimed past Samson at the reader. He thinks it very likely the woman preferred the other man and went to him as soon as her husband had gone home, though she may have thought herself abandoned; her betraying his secret and his interests to his enemies is proof enough that he was not dear to her, whatever crocodile tears she shed to persuade him otherwise. Then the general rule: Samson could not keep his own secret, and was fool enough to suppose another would be more faithful to him than he had been to himself. Multitudes complain of friends who betray their secrets, never considering that they were themselves the first betrayers, in confiding what they pretend to wish concealed from the whole world — for if a man never lets a secret out of his own bosom, it is impossible he should ever be betrayed.
